cards.title: USS Kearny torpedoed
cards.story:
A German torpedo tore into an American warship seven weeks before Pearl Harbor. Eleven sailors never came home.

17 October 1941. Off Iceland, a German wolf pack was savaging a British convoy, and the destroyer USS Kearny raced in with three other U.S. destroyers to help the overwhelmed Canadian escorts. Through the night Kearny dropped depth charges. Then U-568 put a torpedo into her starboard side.

Eleven men were killed and 22 wounded. Her crew sealed off the flooding in the forward fire room and kept her moving on the aft engine. She limped into Iceland at 10 knots two days later.

The United States was not yet at war, but it no longer felt like peace. Ten days later President Roosevelt told the nation, "America has been attacked." Two weeks after Kearny was hit, the USS Reuben James was sunk.
cards.photoCredit: USS Kearny at Reykjavik with the torpedo hole visible midships, 19 October 1941. U.S. Navy 80-G-28788, public domain.

sources.title: USS Kearny (DD-432), Wikipedia

cards.title: Why Kearny stayed afloat
cards.story:
Why didn't USS Kearny sink?

This morning's dispatch told how a U-boat torpedo tore into her off Iceland on 17 October 1941. Part of the answer to how she got home was built into her hull.

Kearny was a Gleaves class destroyer. Her designers split the machinery into two separate units, each with its own fireroom and engine room. The idea was simple: a single torpedo should not be able to cripple the whole ship.

That night it worked. Her crew held the flooding to the forward fire room, and power from the aft fire room carried her out of danger. She reached Iceland two days later.
cards.photoCredit: USS Kearny in Boston Harbor after repairs, 31 March 1942. U.S. Navy Bureau of Ships 19-N-28745, public domain.

sources.title: Kearny (DD-432), Dictionary of American Naval Fighting Ships, Naval History and Heritage Command

cards.title: The Nuremberg indictment is filed
cards.story:
The trial of the century did not begin in Nuremberg. It began with a stack of papers handed across a table in Berlin.

18 October 1945. In the Allied Control Authority Building, the new International Military Tribunal held its first session, with Soviet General Iona Nikitchenko presiding. Prosecutors for the United States, Britain, France, and the Soviet Union each lodged a copy of the indictment.

It named 24 leading Nazis and charged them on four counts: conspiracy, crimes against peace, war crimes, and crimes against humanity. That last charge was new to international law.

The court then moved to Nuremberg, where the trial opened on 20 November 1945. Only 21 men sat in the dock. One had died before trial, one was ruled unfit, and Martin Bormann was tried in absentia.
cards.photoCredit: The opening session of the International Military Tribunal in Berlin, 18 October 1945. Office of the U.S. Chief of Counsel, public domain.

cards.title: German battleship Tirpitz
cards.story:
Can you name this ship?

On 18 October 1944, an RAF reconnaissance plane photographed her at anchor off Tromsø in Norway. By then the British had been trying to sink her for nearly three years.

The clue is on the card. Drop your guess below.
cards.photoCredit: Tirpitz in Bogen Bay, Norway, 1943 to 1944. NHHC NH 71390, public domain.

cards.title: Tojo takes power
cards.story:
Seven weeks before Pearl Harbor, an army general took charge of Japan's government.

18 October 1941. General Hideki Tojo became prime minister. Two days earlier, Prince Konoe had resigned, politically isolated and convinced the emperor no longer trusted him.

Tojo did not give up his old job. He stayed on as Army Minister and took over the Home Ministry too. Colleagues called him "Razor" for his sharp, quick mind.

He took office with orders to re-examine Japan's options for dealing with the United States. On 7 December 1941, Japan attacked Pearl Harbor.
cards.photoCredit: Official portrait of Hideki Tojo, 1941. Public domain.

sources.title: Hideki Tojo, Wikipedia

cards.title: Tin cans go to war
cards.story:
Your kitchen trash was now a weapon of war.

19 October 1942. The War Production Board ordered every American town of more than 25,000 people to set up a tin can collection.

The reason was a map. Nearly 90 percent of America's tin had come from Malaya, and Japan's conquest of Southeast Asia cut that supply almost overnight. Tin was suddenly one of the scarcest metals in the country, and every can thrown away was tin the war effort could not replace.

So families got to work. They peeled off the labels, rinsed the cans, cut out the ends, and stepped them flat. Boy Scouts and other youth groups ran the collections, often once a month, and towns were asked to turn in about a ton of prepared cans for every 1,000 people.

Cans had never been salvaged on a large scale before. Now it was a patriotic duty.
cards.photoCredit: Harry Cardio, 10, of the Gramercy Boys' Club in New York flattens cans for the tin salvage drive, 1942. International News Photos, public domain.

sources.title: Today in World War II History, Oct. 19, 1942, Sarah Sundin
Moment in Time, Gig Harbor Peninsula Historical Society

cards.title: The WAVES open to Black women
cards.story:
For more than two years, the Navy's women's reserve had turned away Black women. On this day that changed.

19 October 1944. With President Roosevelt's approval, the Navy announced that African American women could join the WAVES.

Two of them made history fast. Harriet Ida Pickens and Frances Wills trained at the Naval Reserve Midshipmen's School on the Smith College campus in Northampton, Massachusetts. On 26 December 1944 they were commissioned as the Navy's first Black women officers.

This photo shows them that December, packing up after graduation. Two days later, the first Black enlisted WAVES reported for training at Hunter College in New York.
cards.photoCredit: Harriet Ida Pickens and Frances Wills after graduating from the Naval Reserve Midshipmen's School, Northampton, Massachusetts, December 1944. U.S. Navy 80-G-297441 (NARA), public domain.

sources.title: The Integration of the WAVES and the Navy's First Female African American Officers, Naval History and Heritage Command
Perseverance: Lt. (j.g.) Harriet Ida Pickens and Ensign Frances Wills, U.S. Navy

cards.title: MacArthur returns to Leyte
cards.story:
Two and a half years earlier he had promised, "I shall return." On this day he kept it.

20 October 1944. General Douglas MacArthur rode a landing craft toward Red Beach on Leyte with Philippine President Sergio Osmeña. The boat could not reach dry sand, so they climbed out and waded the last stretch through the surf. Army photographer Gaetano Faillace caught the moment, and it became one of the most famous pictures of the war.

MacArthur had been ordered out of the Philippines in 1942. Arriving in Australia, he told reporters at a railway station, "I came through and I shall return."

Now, standing on Leyte, he spoke into a radio microphone: "People of the Philippines, I have returned!"

The fight for Leyte was only beginning. Within days, the largest naval battle in history would erupt in the waters around it.
cards.photoCredit: General MacArthur and his staff wading ashore at Leyte, 20 October 1944. U.S. Army Signal Corps, Gaetano Faillace, NARA 531424, public domain.

sources.title: Battle of Leyte, Wikipedia
DocsTeach, National Archives

film.caption: Film from Leyte, 20 October 1944. General MacArthur rides a landing craft toward Red Beach with President Sergio Osmeña of the Philippines, then heads inland. U.S. Army Signal Corps footage.

cards.title: A 1944 drone strike
cards.story:
A drone strike, guided by television, in 1944.

20 October 1944. Near Bougainville, Navy drones of Special Task Air Group 1 went after Japanese gun positions on Ballale and a beached cargo ship. One made a good bomb drop on the guns before control was lost. Another straddled the guns, then slammed into the ship almost amidships.

No one was aboard. The TDR-1 was flown by radio from a TBM Avenger that followed it in, where an operator watched a crude TV picture from a camera in the drone's nose.

Its frame was steel tube, reportedly built by the Schwinn bicycle company, under a skin of molded wood. By the end of October 1944 the drones were grounded and the program wound down.
cards.photoCredit: An Interstate TDR-1 assault drone in flight, about 1944. U.S. Navy, public domain.

sources.title: STAG-1 chronology, Pacific Wrecks

cards.title: Aachen surrenders
cards.story:
For the first time in the war, a German city fell to the Allies.

21 October 1944. After five and a half weeks of fighting, the last German garrison in Aachen, holed up in the Hotel Quellenhof, finally surrendered.

Aachen had little military value. What it had was meaning. It was the old capital of Charlemagne, and Nazi propaganda held him up as the founder of Germany's first empire. Hitler ordered the city held at all costs.

The U.S. 1st and 30th Infantry Divisions closed the ring around it, then fought through the ruins house by house, sometimes blasting through walls rather than stepping into the streets. American losses passed 7,000. About 5,600 Germans went into captivity, many marching past the wreckage of the city they had been told to defend.

The road into Germany was open, but it would not be easy.
cards.photoCredit: German prisoners marching through the ruined streets of Aachen, October 1944. NARA 541597, public domain.

sources.title: Battle of Aachen, Wikipedia

film.caption: Film from Aachen, 15 October 1944. Six days before the city surrendered, U.S. Army cameramen filmed the house to house fighting: a tank destroyer firing point blank into a building, infantry going over walls, and a crew pushing an antitank gun through the streets.

cards.title: Boeing B-17 Flying Fortress (B-17D)
cards.clue: Its nickname was all about its guns
cards.story:
Can you name this aircraft?

On 21 October 1942, one of these got lost over the Pacific and ditched at sea. Eight men climbed into life rafts, including America's top fighter ace of the First World War. They drifted for more than three weeks.

The clue is on the card. Drop your guess below.
cards.photoCredit: An early B-17D Flying Fortress at Wright Field, Ohio, about 1941. U.S. Air Force, public domain.

sources.title: B-17D 40-3089, Pacific Wrecks

cards.title: Churchill speaks to France
cards.story:
France had fallen. Britain stood alone. On this night the British prime minister spoke directly to the French people.

21 October 1940. In a BBC broadcast to France, with his notes prepared in both English and French, Winston Churchill opened with a single word: "Frenchmen!"

He spoke to them as old allies, and asked them to keep faith until their country was free. He closed with a promise:

"Good night then: sleep to gather strength for the morning. For the morning will come."

It took nearly four more years. Allied troops landed in Normandy in June 1944, and Paris was liberated that August.
cards.photoCredit: Winston Churchill at his desk, early in his time as prime minister, 1940. British official photograph, Crown copyright expired, public domain.

sources.title: Dieu protege la France, Richard M. Langworth (text of the broadcast)
Churchill Archives Centre, CHAR 9/176A-B (1940 broadcasts, including 21 October to France)

cards.title: Mark Clark's secret landing
cards.story:
An American general paddled ashore in a canoe at night, hid in a wine cellar from the police, and went home without his trousers. It was one of the most important secret meetings of the war.

22 October 1942. Major General Mark Clark landed from the British submarine HMS Seraph near Cherchell, Algeria. At a seaside villa he met French General Charles Mast and U.S. diplomat Robert Murphy. Clark needed the French army in North Africa to help the coming Allied landings, not fight them.

Mast agreed. Then the local police, tipped off by the servants, came knocking. The Americans dropped into the cellar while their hosts faked a drunken party upstairs.

Escaping in heavy surf, Clark stripped off his trousers so the gold coins in his money belt would not drag him under. A canoe was lost, and the gold with it. Clark made it back to Seraph. Seventeen days later came Operation Torch.
cards.photoCredit: HMS Seraph, the submarine that carried Clark to Cherchell, entering harbor with her crew on deck, about 1943. Imperial War Museum, Crown copyright expired, public domain.

sources.title: Operation Flagpole (World War II), Wikipedia
Contact, USNI Naval History, April 2023 (HMS Seraph photo, credit Imperial War Museum)

cards.title: This Is the Army takes its last bow
cards.story:
Irving Berlin wrote a show for soldiers, starring soldiers, and took it from Broadway all the way to the Pacific. On this day it played for the last time.

22 October 1945. This Is the Army gave its final performance in Hawaii. Berlin stepped out and sang "Oh! How I Hate to Get Up in the Morning," the song from his own 1918 Army show, Yip Yip Yaphank.

The show had opened on Broadway on 4 July 1942 with a cast of 300 soldiers. Its proceeds went to Army Emergency Relief.

Berlin insisted on including Black soldiers, and the company was described as the only fully integrated outfit in the U.S. Army, except on stage.
cards.photoCredit: Irving Berlin, in his First World War uniform, backstage with soldiers at This Is the Army, about 1943. U.S. Army Signal Corps 111-SC-279543, public domain.

sources.title: This Is the Army (musical), Wikipedia
This Is the Army (film), Wikipedia

cards.title: The barrage at El Alamein
cards.story:
At 9:40 p.m. the desert lit up like day.

23 October 1942. Nearly 900 British and Commonwealth guns opened fire at once along the line at El Alamein in Egypt. It was the start of Operation Lightfoot, and the noise rolled across the sand for miles.

Behind the barrage, Montgomery's Eighth Army began clearing paths through the minefields the Germans called the Devil's Gardens.

The timing was cruel for the other side. Rommel was in Germany on sick leave. His stand in, General Georg Stumme, died of a heart attack the next day while driving to the front. Rommel flew back to a battle already underway.

Twelve days later, on 4 November, he ordered the retreat. Back in London, Churchill told the country it was perhaps "the end of the beginning."
cards.photoCredit: A 25 pounder gun firing during the night barrage that opened the Second Battle of El Alamein, 23 October 1942. IWM E 18469, Crown copyright expired, public domain.

sources.title: Second Battle of El Alamein, Wikipedia

film.caption: Film from El Alamein, 23 October 1942. At 9:40 p.m. nearly 900 British and Commonwealth guns opened fire, and army cameramen filmed the flashes in the dark. From the 1943 British documentary Desert Victory.

cards.title: The Sherman's first battle
cards.story:
Behind this morning's barrage at El Alamein waited a new weapon: the American built Sherman tank.

23 October 1942. As the Eighth Army opened its offensive, 252 Shermans stood ready. At dawn the next day they went into battle for the first time.

Crews liked the 75 mm gun, which hit hard and was easy to load. They liked the high mounted gun too, which let a tank hide behind a dune with only its turret showing. The gun sight they could do without.

The other side noticed. A captured German document called it a vehicle with "incredible armor and very good armament."

More than 49,000 Shermans would be built. Their war started here.
cards.photoCredit: Sherman II tanks of the Queen's Bays moving up to the Alamein line, 24 October 1942. IWM E 18380, Crown copyright expired, public domain.

sources.title: Sherman's African Debut, Tank Archives
M4 Sherman, Wikipedia

cards.title: UN Charter takes effect
cards.story:
The world had just survived its deadliest war. On this day, a new organization was built to stop the next one.

24 October 1945. The United Nations Charter took effect, once China, France, the Soviet Union, the United Kingdom, and the United States had ratified it, along with a majority of the other signers.

Fifty nations had signed the Charter in San Francisco that June. Poland, not represented at the conference, signed in October, making 51 founding members. Its opening words still echo: "We the peoples of the United Nations."

The League of Nations had failed to stop the road to war in the 1930s. The UN was designed with a stronger Security Council and a permanent seat for each of the great powers that won the war.

October 24 is still marked every year as United Nations Day.
cards.photoCredit: Wartime poster quoting the opening words of the United Nations Charter. NARA 516086, public domain.

sources.title: Charter of the United Nations, Wikipedia

cards.title: Japanese battleship Musashi
cards.clue: Her sister was even more famous
cards.story:
Can you name this ship?

She left Brunei in October 1944, bound for the largest naval battle in history. On 24 October, American carrier planes caught her in the Sibuyan Sea.

The clue is on the card. Drop your guess below.
cards.photoCredit: Musashi leaving Brunei on her last voyage, October 1944. NHHC NH 63473, public domain.

sources.title: Japanese battleship Musashi, Wikipedia

cards.title: First photo of Earth from space
cards.story:
This grainy picture was taken from a Nazi weapon, over New Mexico, and it is the first photo of Earth from space.

24 October 1946. At White Sands, scientists launched a captured German V-2 rocket with a 35mm movie camera bolted into its nose. The rocket climbed about 65 miles, far higher than any airplane or balloon, and filmed the Earth below as it rose.

Then it fell back, hitting the desert at roughly 500 feet per second. The rocket was wrecked. But the film had been sealed inside a steel case.

A recovery team drove out into the desert to find it, including 19 year old Fred Rulli. The film was intact. When the footage was first shown, he later recalled, the scientists were overjoyed.

The rockets built to bomb London had given humanity its first look back at home.
cards.photoCredit: The first photograph of Earth from space, taken by a camera aboard a V-2 rocket over White Sands, New Mexico, 24 October 1946. U.S. Army, public domain.

sources.title: Smithsonian Magazine

cards.title: The last stand of Taffy 3
cards.story:
Six small escort carriers and seven little warships looked to the horizon at dawn and saw the biggest battleship in the world coming for them.

25 October 1944. Off the island of Samar, an American group called Taffy 3 was there to fly air support for the troops on Leyte, not to fight battleships. Then Admiral Takeo Kurita's Center Force appeared: four battleships, including the giant Yamato, six heavy cruisers, two light cruisers, and eleven destroyers.

Rear Admiral Clifton Sprague ordered smoke, turned away, and called for help. His three destroyers and four destroyer escorts turned the other way and charged the battleships, firing torpedoes from close range. Planes from the little carriers attacked again and again.

It cost Taffy 3 two carriers, two destroyers, and a destroyer escort. Then, at 9:20, Kurita ordered his fleet north and broke off the battle. That same morning, the first organized kamikaze attacks hit the escort carriers, and one sank St. Lo.
cards.photoCredit: USS Gambier Bay and her escorts making smoke during the Battle off Samar, 25 October 1944. U.S. Navy, public domain.

sources.title: Battle off Samar, Wikipedia

Wreck of USS Johnston discovered, Military Times

film.caption: U.S. Navy film from the Battle off Samar, 25 October 1944. A plane launches from an escort carrier, then Japanese shells throw up splashes among the little ships of Taffy 3.

cards.title: The destroyer that charged
cards.story:
Of the 327 men aboard USS Johnston that morning, only 141 came home. Their captain had promised them a fighting ship.

25 October 1944. When Japanese battleships appeared off Samar, Commander Ernest E. Evans turned his destroyer toward them and charged, laying smoke and firing torpedoes at the heavy cruiser Kumano. At least one hit, and Kumano lost her bow.

Evans, of Cherokee and Creek heritage, had told the crew at her commissioning a year earlier: "This is going to be a fighting ship."

A shell hit the bridge and took two fingers from his hand. Johnston kept fighting until she sank. Evans was never seen again, and he received the Medal of Honor. Her wreck was found more than 20,000 feet down.
cards.photoCredit: USS Johnston underway on her commissioning day, 27 October 1943. NHHC NH 63495, public domain.

cards.title: Hornet's last fight
cards.story:
Six months after she carried the Doolittle Raiders to bomb Tokyo, USS Hornet was fighting for her life.

26 October 1942. Near the Santa Cruz Islands, American and Japanese carriers traded air strikes in the long fight for Guadalcanal. In the morning attack, a Japanese dive bomber trailing smoke struck Hornet's stack. Bombs and torpedoes hit her too, and soon the carrier was dead in the water.

This photo catches that dive, a single plane coming down through a sky full of bursting flak.

American destroyers tried to sink the wrecked carrier with torpedoes and gunfire. She would not go down. That night Japanese destroyers arrived and finished her.

On paper Japan won the day. It sank a carrier and damaged Enterprise. But it lost about 100 aircraft and many of its most experienced crews, and its carriers were out of action when the decisive naval battle at Guadalcanal came less than three weeks later.
cards.photoCredit: A Japanese dive bomber trails smoke as it dives on USS Hornet, 26 October 1942. U.S. Navy 80-G-33947 (NARA), public domain.

sources.title: The United States loses the Hornet, HISTORY

cards.title: The Mustang's first flight
cards.story:
In 1940 Britain was fighting for its life and needed fighters fast. It asked an American company to build someone else's design. The company offered to build a better one.

26 October 1940. Test pilot Vance Breese took the prototype, the NA-73X, into the air for the first time at Mines Field in Los Angeles. It had gone from order to rollout in less than four months.

Britain had already ordered 320 and called it the Mustang. Its Allison engine lost power up high, so the RAF flew the first Mustangs low, on reconnaissance and ground attack.

Fitted later with the Rolls-Royce Merlin, the Mustang could escort bombers from England deep into Germany and back. More than 15,000 were built.
cards.photoCredit: The NA-73X prototype, NX19998, in 1940. North American Aviation photo, public domain.

sources.title: North American P-51 Mustang, Wikipedia

cards.title: The guns at Outpost Snipe
cards.story:
Nineteen small antitank guns, dug into a desert hollow in the dark. At dawn the enemy's tanks came at them, and they kept coming all day.

27 October 1942. Four days into the Second Battle of El Alamein, the 2nd Battalion of the Rifle Brigade and a battery of Royal Artillery gunners held a position codenamed Snipe. Their guns were six pounders. Through the day, German and Italian tanks attacked again and again.

Their commander, Lieutenant Colonel Victor Turner, found one gun down to an officer and a sergeant, and joined them as loader. Between them they knocked out five more tanks. A shell fragment hit Turner in the head. He would not let anyone treat it until the last tank had been driven off.

A month later, a committee walked the ground and counted between 52 and 57 enemy armored vehicles knocked out around Snipe. Turner received the Victoria Cross.

Eight days after Snipe, the British broke through at El Alamein, and Rommel's army began its long retreat.
cards.photoCredit: A 6 pounder anti tank gun in the Western Desert, 29 October 1942. IWM E 18802, Crown copyright expired, public domain.

sources.title: Defence of Outpost Snipe, Wikipedia

cards.title: The shooting has started
cards.story:
Ten days after a U-boat torpedoed USS Kearny, the President told the country what it meant.

27 October 1941. In his Navy Day address from the Mayflower Hotel in Washington, Franklin D. Roosevelt spoke of the destroyer hit off Iceland, where eleven of her sailors died. "America has been attacked," he said. "The U.S.S. Kearny is not just a Navy ship. She belongs to every man, woman, and child in this Nation."

Then he said:

"We have wished to avoid shooting. But the shooting has started. And history has recorded who fired the first shot."

Four days later, a U-boat sank USS Reuben James. Pearl Harbor was six weeks away.
cards.photoCredit: Franklin D. Roosevelt, portrait by Elias Goldensky, 1933. Public domain.

sources.title: Address for Navy and Total Defense Day, American Presidency Project

cards.title: Greece says no
cards.story:
At three in the morning, Italy's ambassador arrived unannounced at the home of Greece's prime minister with an ultimatum. The answer took one sentence.

28 October 1940. Emanuele Grazzi handed Ioannis Metaxas a demand from Mussolini: let Italian troops occupy strategic places in Greece, or face war. Metaxas had three hours to decide. He replied in French: "Alors, c'est la guerre." Well then, it is war.

Italian troops crossed the border from Albania at 5:30 a.m., before the deadline had even run out.

Greeks soon boiled his reply down to a single word, Ochi, meaning no. Mussolini expected an easy win. Instead the outnumbered Greek army stopped the invasion by mid November, then pushed the Italians back deep into Albania.

Greece still marks 28 October every year as Ochi Day, one of its two national days.
cards.photoCredit: Ioannis Metaxas, prime minister of Greece, 1937. Public domain.

cards.title: Clark Gable
cards.story:
Can you name this man?

On this day in 1942, he finished officer school at Miami Beach and was commissioned a second lieutenant in the Army Air Forces. He had enlisted as a private that August, at 41. He went on to fly combat missions over Europe as a gunner and observer in B-17s.

The clue is on the card. Drop your guess below.

cards.title: Rommel's counterattack broken
cards.story:
Rommel gathered his panzers for one more blow at El Alamein. The bombers found them first.

28 October 1942. Rommel's 15th and 21st Panzer Divisions attacked the British line near Kidney Ridge and were stopped by gun and tank fire. That afternoon they massed to try again. Allied aircraft bombed them as they formed up, and the second attack never got going.

Rommel never seized the initiative at El Alamein again. Within a week, his army was in retreat.
cards.photoCredit: B-25 bombers on a mission over the Western Desert, Egypt, late 1942. U.S. Air Force 23326 A.C. (NARA 204943770), public domain.

cards.title: America's draft lottery
cards.story:
A blindfolded man reached into a giant glass bowl in Washington, and millions of young American men waited to hear their number.

29 October 1940. Two weeks after registration day, the government drew the lottery for America's first peacetime draft. Every registered man had a number. Now the order they would be called in came out of a bowl last used for the draft of the First World War.

Secretary of War Henry Stimson, blindfolded, pulled out the first capsule. President Franklin D. Roosevelt read the number aloud: 158.

Families listened on the radio, and newspapers printed every number as fast as it came in. Cartoonist Clifford Berryman drew the scene that day with Mars, the god of war, at the bowl and Uncle Sam waiting his turn.

The men called that winter expected to serve one year. Thirteen months later came Pearl Harbor.
cards.photoCredit: Secretary of War Henry L. Stimson, blindfolded, draws the first capsule of the draft lottery as President Roosevelt looks on, Washington, 29 October 1940. Harris and Ewing Collection, Library of Congress, public domain.

cards.title: The draft by the numbers
cards.story:
When the first number came out of the bowl, 6,175 men across America found out they held it.

29 October 1940. The lottery put into motion the Selective Training and Service Act, which President Roosevelt had signed on 16 September. It created the first peacetime draft in American history. Men from 21 to 35 registered. Those chosen served twelve months, no more than 900,000 could be in training at once, and they could serve only in the Western Hemisphere or American territory.

The one year limit did not last. In August 1941 the House voted to extend service by a single vote, 203 to 202. Four months later, the country was at war.
cards.photoCredit: President Roosevelt signs the Selective Training and Service Act, 16 September 1940. Public domain.

cards.title: Rescue of the Lost Battalion
cards.story:
To reach 211 trapped Texans, a unit of Japanese American soldiers paid with hundreds of casualties of its own.

30 October 1944. In the cold, wet forests of the Vosges Mountains in eastern France, the 1st Battalion of the 141st Infantry had been cut off by German troops since 24 October. About 275 men were surrounded.

The 442nd Regimental Combat Team was sent to get them out. It was a segregated unit of Nisei, the American born sons of Japanese immigrants, and it had been pulled out of a rest after liberating the towns of Bruyères and Biffontaine. For days its men attacked uphill through German positions in the trees.

On 30 October they broke through. 211 men of the Lost Battalion walked out.

By most counts the 442nd took more casualties in the rescue than the number of men it saved. In 1962 Texas made its veterans honorary Texans.

cards.title: The codebooks of U-559
cards.story:
Two British sailors climbed down into a sinking U-boat to steal its secrets. Neither of them came back out.

30 October 1942. Off Port Said, Egypt, the destroyer HMS Petard and other ships forced U-559 to the surface after hours of depth charge attacks. As the German crew abandoned the boat, Lieutenant Tony Fasson and Able Seaman Colin Grazier went aboard and below. Tommy Brown, a teenage canteen assistant who had lied about his age to serve, followed them.

They passed up codebooks, including the short weather cipher. Then U-559 sank, taking Fasson and Grazier with her. Brown survived.

Bletchley Park had been locked out of the U-boat code for more than ten months. With these books, it broke back in on 13 December 1942.

cards.title: Reuben James is sunk
cards.story:
Five weeks before Pearl Harbor, a U-boat torpedo blew an American destroyer in two.

31 October 1941. USS Reuben James was escorting convoy HX 156 toward Britain near Iceland when U-552 fired at dawn. The torpedo was meant for a merchant ship. It struck the destroyer forward instead, and her magazine exploded, tearing off the bow.

The bow sank at once. As the stern went down, its depth charges went off among the men in the water. Only 44 of her crew survived, pulled from the sea by the destroyers Niblack and Hilary P. Jones. Not one officer was among them.

The United States was not yet at war. Reuben James was the first U.S. Navy ship sunk by enemy action in the war against Germany, four days after President Roosevelt had said, "The shooting has started."

Woody Guthrie wrote a song about her.

cards.title: de Havilland Mosquito (FB.VI)
cards.story:
Can you name this aircraft?

On this day in 1944, 25 of these twin engine fighter bombers struck the Gestapo headquarters at Aarhus University in occupied Denmark, at the request of the Danish resistance. They came in so low that one pilot hit part of the building. The Gestapo offices were destroyed.

The clue is on the card. Drop your guess below.

cards.title: Mount Rushmore's last day
cards.story:
For fourteen years, nearly 400 workers rode down a granite cliff on steel cables to carve it with dynamite. Not one of them died.

31 October 1941. Work on Mount Rushmore came to an end. Gutzon Borglum, the sculptor who designed it, had died that March, and his son Lincoln Borglum carried the job to its finish.

About 90 percent of the carving was done with dynamite, blasting until only inches of rock were left. Workers climbed 700 stairs to the top each morning, then were lowered over the face in bosun chairs. One remembered the pay as $8 a day.

Five weeks later came Pearl Harbor.
